title: Building The New Equilibrium Economy | NOEMA
gist: Philipp Humm argues that AI and robotics could cut labor demand by roughly 30% just as Western populations shrink by about 30% by 2100, a '30/30 equilibrium' that turns demographic decline into a stabilizer; with ~45% higher capital productivity, GDP per capita could rise over 40% while aggregate GDP stays flat, letting societies 'shrink rich'. He rejects debt- or tax-funded UBI as inflationary and proposes a universal capital dividend from public equity stakes in AI infrastructure, while warning that meaninglessness and atrophying human judgment are the deeper post-labor risks.

insights.claim: Advanced economies are simultaneously spending heavily to offset labor shortages (family subsidies, immigration) while investing in AI technologies designed to eliminate labor, a policy contradiction the author sees as defining the moment.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Policy aimed at preserving labor-force size may be fighting the same structural shift that AI capex is accelerating.
insights.quote: Never before has a society simultaneously spent so much money attempting to compensate for labor shortages while investing so much in technologies designed to eliminate labor altogether.

insights.claim: UN projections suggest that, with current fertility and zero net migration, many Western populations will shrink by about 30% by 2100, with Italy's decline approaching 40%-50%.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Italy is the extreme case for any thesis linking depopulation to automation-driven labor demand.
insights.quote: many Western populations will shrink by about 30% by the end of this century

insights.claim: Immigration's fiscal contribution depends on skills: highly skilled migrants (a minority) tend to generate net gains, while low-skilled immigration (the majority) can be a net fiscal drag on advanced welfare states.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Mass immigration is a weak fiscal fix for aging welfare states unless skewed to high-skill inflows.

insights.claim: Silicon Valley figures such as Elon Musk and Peter Thiel warn that collapsing birth rates threaten civilization even as their companies build systems that reduce the economy's dependence on human labor.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Tech pronatalism sits uneasily with tech's own labor-replacing business models.

insights.claim: South Korea, with fertility around 0.75 and tens of billions a year spent on birth incentives with little success, has become the world's most robot-intensive economy at over 1,000 industrial robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Korea is the live test case of automation substituting for a collapsing workforce.
insights.quote: South Korea has become the most robot-intensive economy in the world with over 1,000 industrial robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers

insights.claim: Japan, whose working-age population has declined for over two decades, has more than 400 industrial robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers versus a world average of roughly 120-150.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Robot density tracks demographic decline; demographic decliners are the leading automation adopters.

insights.claim: The author frames South Korea and Japan as a preview of the intelligence economy and asks whether demographic decline and automation could become complementary rather than opposing forces.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Watch East Asia for evidence that shrinking workforces plus automation can sustain output.
insights.quote: Could demographic decline and automation eventually become complementary rather than opposing forces?
insights.locator: South Korea and Japan offer a preview

themes.theme: Wage-labor architecture of the welfare state

insights.claim: The labor-centred society is a modern invention rather than an anthropological constant; per Hannah Arendt, modernity overturned the classical hierarchy in which labor was a necessity, not life's purpose, and Adam Smith located national wealth in productive labor.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Post-labor policy debates need not assume work-centred identity is permanent.
insights.quote: The labor society as we know it today is not an anthropological constant.

insights.claim: Industrial capitalism bound production, wages and demand together, symbolized by Henry Ford's 1914 wage increase so workers could buy the cars they built; around 1800 roughly 75% of Americans worked in agriculture versus fewer than 2% today.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: The wage-demand loop is the mechanism AI threatens to break.
insights.quote: production, wages and demand were bound together

insights.claim: In OECD nations labor accounts for up to 60% of GDP and private consumption nearly 70%, and wages fund taxation, welfare and pensions while serving as the main mechanism of social integration.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Any large erosion of labor income hits both fiscal bases and the consumption share of GDP.
insights.quote: labor accounts for up to 60% of GDP and private consumption for nearly 70% for OECD nations
insights.locator: This model was at the core

insights.claim: Every productive hour of paid work finances about nine hours of non-working life across society (childhood, education, retirement, evenings, illness), and this ratio has risen with shorter working hours and longer life expectancy.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Dependency ratios are already stretched before any AI displacement.
insights.quote: Every productive hour finances about nine hours of non-working life

insights.claim: Advanced economies have so far answered how to finance ever more years of life with ever fewer years of work through a fragile mix of economic growth and rising public debt, which AI-driven labor-market erosion could undermine.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Sovereign fiscal sustainability is exposed if AI shrinks the wage tax base.
insights.quote: How does a society finance ever more years of life with ever fewer years of work?

themes.theme: AI makes intelligence abundant and labor non-scarce

insights.claim: Each technological revolution made a scarce factor abundant: the Industrial Revolution cheapened mechanical energy via fossil fuels, 1990s-2000s globalization cheapened physical labor via China, and AI may now do the same to intelligence.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Frame AI as a factor-price shock to cognition, with winners among owners of the newly abundant input.

insights.claim: The historical adjustment mechanism of Schumpeterian creative destruction, whereby new jobs replace destroyed ones, may no longer apply to AI because, per Erik Brynjolfsson's 'Turing Trap', AI performs the cognitive tasks that once let workers move up the value chain.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: The 'new jobs always emerge' assumption underpinning official forecasts is fragile.
insights.quote: With AI, this historical adjustment mechanism may no longer be applicable.

insights.claim: Following Daron Acemoglu, whether AI destroys net employment depends on firms choosing replacement over augmentation, and the structure of today's most valuable AI companies, with huge market value and remarkably small workforces, already reflects the replacement logic.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Value creation in AI is decoupled from employment, concentrating returns in capital.
insights.quote: Many of today’s most valuable AI companies generate extraordinary market value with remarkably small workforces.

insights.claim: Agentic AI accelerates substitution because agents perform entire workflows, analyzing information, correcting errors, adapting strategies and coordinating processes, rather than isolated tasks.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Workflow-level automation widens the addressable labor pool beyond task-level tools.

insights.claim: In the first, white-collar wave, a junior analyst, lawyer, consultant or engineer in London or New York may cost 80-100 per hour while language models perform many of their tasks for a fraction of a cent, and software improvements propagate instantly across an organization unlike human knowledge that leaves with employees.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Cost gaps of several orders of magnitude make entry-level professional roles most exposed first.
insights.quote: Modern language models can already perform many of their tasks for a fraction of a cent.

insights.claim: In the second, blue-collar wave, humanoid robot makers such as Tesla and Unitree hope to cut operating costs below $2 per hour versus 30-50 per hour for an average American worker.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: If humanoid cost targets are met, physical labor faces the same arbitrage as cognitive labor.
insights.quote: Their manufacturers hope eventually to reduce operating costs to below $2 per hour.
insights.locator: The second wave is now reaching

insights.claim: Citing IMF research that nearly 60% of jobs in advanced economies will be affected by AI, with almost half facing substantial disruption or substitution, the author judges a roughly 30% fall in total employment over coming decades plausible, with the exact 20%-40% figure secondary.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Planning scenarios should include double-digit structural employment declines.
insights.quote: a reduction of roughly 30% in total employment over the coming decades no longer appears implausible
insights.locator: Research by the International Monetary Fund

insights.claim: The author's '30/30 equilibrium' posits that a roughly 30% population decline over decades and a similar AI-driven fall in labor demand could broadly offset each other, keeping the ratio of productive labor to population stable without extra fiscal burden.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Depopulation could be recast from macro risk to adjustment mechanism, changing the bear case for aging economies.
insights.quote: Fewer people require fewer jobs.

insights.claim: The 30/30 equilibrium only stabilizes the macroeconomy; whether a shrinking society gets richer depends on capital deepening, since per the Solow-Swan model long-run prosperity depends on capital per worker rather than labor-force size.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Per-capita, not aggregate, GDP becomes the relevant metric for shrinking AI economies.
insights.locator: Whether a shrinking society also becomes richer

insights.claim: Offsetting a 30% labor-force decline to hold GDP flat would require roughly a 45% rise in capital productivity, which would lift GDP per capita by over 40%, a gain the author considers not particularly ambitious given learning curves in semiconductors, compute, AI and robotics.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Flat aggregate GDP can coexist with strong per-capita gains, so headline growth may mislead.
insights.quote: A 30% decline in the labor force would have to be offset by roughly a 45% increase in capital productivity.
insights.locator: If we want an economy’s GDP to stabilize

insights.claim: With a constant population, the same 45% increase in productive capital would expand total output by roughly 20%, which conventional economics would celebrate as superior, though the author argues otherwise.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: The author rejects aggregate growth as the success metric.
insights.quote: Conventional economics would celebrate this as the superior outcome.

insights.claim: Jevons' paradox implies that cheaper AI will lead to far more AI consumption, so Silicon Valley's 'abundance' is not necessarily environmentally sustainable given AI's need for electricity, compute infrastructure, rare materials and hardware.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Falling AI costs likely raise total energy and materials demand rather than reduce it.
insights.quote: As AI becomes cheaper, we will almost certainly consume far more of it.

insights.claim: Letting populations decline naturally while raising prosperity per person may be a superior equilibrium environmentally, and the author argues the 21st-century goal should be to maximize prosperity rather than growth: to 'shrink rich'.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Reframes demographic decline in developed markets as potentially compatible with rising living standards.
insights.quote: The ambition of the 21st century should no longer be to maximize growth but to maximize prosperity: to shrink rich.

insights.claim: Drawing on ecologist Eugene Odum's pioneer versus climax ecosystems, the author casts the fossil-fuel economy as humanity's expansionary pioneer phase and suggests AI plus demographic decline could enable a mature 'climax society', with robotic recycling, AI-managed precision fermentation and closed material loops as early signs.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Circular-material and precision-fermentation technologies fit the low-input prosperity thesis.

themes.theme: Financial and geopolitical assumptions to abandon

insights.claim: Modern debt, money creation and asset valuations depend on continual expansion, so a shrinking-rich economy may require a monetary and financial system that derives stability from growing capital productivity rather than ever-expanding debt.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Shrinking-population economies challenge debt-dependent asset valuation frameworks.
insights.quote: Tomorrow’s economy must become larger than today’s because yesterday’s obligations must be repaid.

insights.claim: The 'big is beautiful' geopolitical logic of scale is eroding because AI makes usable intelligence abundant and technologies like autonomous drones erode traditional military advantages of large populations, with the same true for economic influence.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Population size may matter less for national power, narrowing the advantage of large states.

themes.theme: Who captures the AI surplus: UBI vs capital dividend

insights.claim: Under the existing order, AI productivity gains will accrue mainly to owners of capital, shifting income from wages to owners of machines, models, data centers, energy systems and platforms.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Supports a structural shift in factor share from labor to AI-infrastructure owners.

insights.claim: If machines produce while humans lose wages, the demand side weakens, so even the most productive AI economy depends on customers who can afford its output, a problem for capital owners themselves.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Labor-share collapse is a demand risk for AI beneficiaries, not just a distributional issue.
insights.quote: Even the most productive AI economy ultimately depends on customers who can afford to buy what it produces.

insights.claim: Universal basic income financed by public debt or production taxes is inflationary, adding purchasing power without productive assets or being passed into higher prices, and so dissipates much of AI's productivity dividend; the author calls it a pharmakon, remedy and poison at once.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Debt-funded UBI regimes would carry inflation risk that erodes real gains from AI.
insights.quote: UBI risks becoming a pharmakon: remedy and poison at the same time.

insights.claim: The 1795 Speenhamland wage supplement in England ended up subsidizing employers who kept wages low and entrenched the poor's dependence on local authorities, a warning that income support is unlikely to be a durable post-labor foundation.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Historical precedent suggests transfer schemes can be captured by employers.

insights.claim: Because AI models are trained on humanity's accumulated knowledge and rely on publicly funded research and infrastructure, echoing Marx's 'general intellect', the author argues society has a claim on AI's productive infrastructure.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Raises the political case for public claims on AI firms built on commons data.
insights.quote: The intelligence economy is built by both private firms and a civilizational commons.

insights.claim: The author proposes a universal capital dividend instead of UBI: governments take equity, public or sovereign wealth stakes in AI infrastructure and distribute proceeds directly to citizens, which he argues is non-inflationary because it distributes gains at source.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Signals potential policy pressure for state equity stakes in AI infrastructure.
insights.quote: The intelligence economy may ultimately solve it through ownership.
insights.locator: The 20th century solved the demand problem

themes.theme: Meaning and judgment in a post-labor society

insights.claim: Following Arendt's warning of 'worldlessness' and Graeber's 'bullshit jobs', the author argues the deeper post-labor crisis may be meaninglessness rather than unemployment, since societies have forgotten how to organize meaning outside paid work.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Social stability in AI transitions depends on non-economic institutions, not just income.
insights.quote: The deeper crisis of the post-labor age may therefore not be unemployment, but meaninglessness.

insights.claim: Delegation to AI progresses from assisting to recommending to deciding, and each rational delegation, in navigation, finance, partner selection and legal decisions, can atrophy human judgment, which the author calls perhaps the deepest alignment problem: confusing machine optimization with human judgment.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Dependency on AI decision systems is a creeping systemic risk beyond job loss.
insights.quote: Every delegation begins as a convenience and may end in dependency.
insights.locator: The second challenge is even more
